nameStory: The name 'pochard' comes from the French word 'pochard,' which originally meant 'drunkard' - perhaps referring to the duck's tendency to tip forward while diving for food, resembling someone who's had too much to drink! The 'common' part simply distinguishes it from other pochard species, though ironically this duck is anything but common in New England.
description: The Common Pochard is a medium-sized diving duck that's built for underwater adventures. Males sport a distinctive rusty-red head and neck that contrasts beautifully with their black chest and pale gray back, while females wear more subdued brown plumage overall. These compact ducks are slightly smaller than a Mallard, with a rounded profile that helps them slip beneath the water's surface to hunt for aquatic plants and small creatures.

idTips.label: Male's rusty-red head
idTips.description: Breeding males have a rich, coppery-red head and neck that looks almost burnished in sunlight - much redder than a Redhead's orange-tinged head

idTips.label: Diving behavior
idTips.description: Watch them disappear completely underwater with a quick forward plunge, staying submerged for 15-30 seconds while foraging

idTips.label: Bill shape
idTips.description: Both sexes have a broad, flattened bill with a distinctive black band across the tip that feels smooth if handled

idTips.label: Body profile
idTips.description: Compact and rounded when floating, sitting lower in the water than dabbling ducks like Mallards

idTips.label: Female coloring
idTips.description: Females are warm brown overall with a paler, grayish face and neck that has a subtle mottled texture

habitat: Common Pochards are extremely rare visitors to New England, typically appearing on large, deep freshwater lakes and reservoirs during migration or winter. When they do show up, look for them on bodies of water with abundant submerged vegetation like pondweed and wild celery, often in the company of other diving ducks like Canvasback or Redhead.

seasonality.spring: Extremely rare spring migrants might pass through in April or May, often mixed in with flocks of other diving ducks heading to northern breeding grounds.
seasonality.summer: Not expected in New England during breeding season, as they nest primarily in northern Europe and Asia.
seasonality.fall: The best chance to spot one is during fall migration from October through November, when a lost bird might turn up on a large lake.
seasonality.winter: Occasionally a vagrant individual winters on ice-free portions of large lakes or coastal ponds, associating with other diving ducks.

funFact: Common Pochards are such accomplished divers that they can forage in water up to 12 feet deep, and females sometimes build their nests on floating mats of vegetation that rise and fall with changing water levels - nature's own floating dock!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with the much more common Redhead, but male Common Pochards have a deeper, rustier red head (not orange-red) and lack the Redhead's yellow eyes. Female pochards are browner overall compared to the grayer female Redhead.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'Common' Pochard, this European species is incredibly rare in North America - so rare that any sighting in New England would be a major birding event worth reporting to eBird and local birding communities.
compareHints: Among its Aythya relatives in New England, male Common Pochards most resemble Redheads but have deeper red heads and darker eyes. They're more compact than Canvasback and lack the sloped profile, while being larger and more colorful than scaups. The rusty-red head color is unique among regularly occurring New England diving ducks.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its Aythya relatives, Ring-necked Duck is the small, vegetarian cousin with the white bill ring.
Compared to Ring-necked Ducks, Greater Scaup lack the white ring around the bill and have much more white on their sides and back.
Among New England's diving ducks in the same genus, Lesser Scaup are most similar to Greater Scaup but have rounder heads and shorter wing stripes.

Among its Aythya relatives in New England, the Redhead's rounded head shape sets it apart from the wedge-headed Canvasback, while its copper (not dark) head distinguishes it from Ring-necked Ducks and scaups.
Among its diving duck relatives, canvasbacks are much larger than ring-necked ducks and scaup, with that unique sloping head profile no other Aythya duck shares.
Among its Aythya relatives, Tufted Duck is most similar to Ring-necked Duck but has the distinctive drooping head tuft and golden (not yellow) eyes.
